intro.overview: Welcome to NEXUS Security Consulting. In this foundational lab, you will deploy your personal security operations platform using Kali Linux in a virtualized environment. This setup will serve as your primary workspace for all hands-on exercises throughout the semester. You'll learn to configure virtual machines, install Docker for containerized client targets, and verify your environment is ready for purple team operations.
objectives: Deploy Kali Linux as your security operations platform
Install and verify Docker for containerized client targets
Document your environment for your Module 1 Engagement Packet
focusAreas: Kali Linux as a purpose-built security testing platform
Docker container fundamentals and container vs. VM differences

clientContext.description: Dallas-based wealth management firm ($2.8B AUM, 450 employees) facing an SEC cybersecurity examination in six months. Your Module 1 engagement begins with internal training: you'll build the analyst workstation and toolkit you'll use for the Brazos network reconnaissance assessment in Unit 3.

callouts.title: Use the Hypervisor That Fits Your Computer
callouts.text:
This course doesn’t tell you which hypervisor to use. Your computer decides that. Checkpoint 1 gives you the requirements your Kali VM has to meet and the options with what they cost. You describe your computer to the AI assistant you use, it recommends the best fit, and then it tailors the setup steps to the hypervisor you choose. That is a real use of AI: turning a general spec into steps for your own machine.

What is graded is the outcome: a working Kali VM that meets the requirements, named with your abc123, and the evidence you’re asked to capture.

callouts.title: Technically Droppable, Actually Required
callouts.text: Lab 1.1 is one of ten Training Labs, and you do get one drop. So administratively, yes, you could skip this one and have it not count against your grade. But practically, you can’t skip it. Lab 1.2 needs your Kali VM running. So do EP 1, Labs 2.1, 2.2, every lab through Module 5. Skip Lab 1.1 and you’ll have to come back and do it anyway before Lab 1.2 is due, except now your drop is gone and the deadline is tighter. Use your drop on a lab that doesn’t gate everything that follows it.

callouts.title: Save For EP 1
callouts.text: This is Unit 1 of a 3-unit module. Create a folder called Module1_Screenshots and save EVERY screenshot there. You'll compile these into your Module 1 Engagement Packet in Unit 3.

mentorQuote.title: Senior Penetration Tester, NEXUS Security
mentorQuote.quote: Every analyst at NEXUS starts here: building their own lab environment. This isn't just homework; it's your personal security workstation. Treat it like your toolkit. You'll use this setup for every client engagement this semester. Document everything. Your future self will thank you when you're writing runbooks at 2 AM.

rows.task: Checkpoint 1: Choose and install your hypervisor

timeGuide.timesheetNote: This is Unit 1 of 3. Log these hours as Internal Training on your EP 1 timesheet. Save every screenshot to your Module1_Screenshots folder. You’ll need them all in Unit 3.

content.whatYoureDoing: Choosing the hypervisor that fits your computer, with an AI assistant’s help, and installing it.
content.whyItMatters: Virtual machines allow you to run a complete operating system inside your existing OS. This is how security professionals maintain isolated environments for testing tools, malware analysis, and client engagements without risking their primary system.

content.title: Your Computer Comes First
content.body: The Information Systems and Cybersecurity department requires you to own a laptop that meets its minimum device requirements. Every lab in this course runs on the VM you build here, so check your computer against that page before you start. If you don’t have access to a suitable machine, start with the options on that page, including the one-time financial aid adjustment for technology, and email me right away at john.newsom@utsa.edu so we can get you sorted as soon as possible. Don’t wait until the lab is due.

content.title: What Your VM Has to Be
content.body:
Whichever hypervisor you use, your Kali VM has to meet every one of these. They are the same for everyone.
  • Kali image: the official installer for your processor: amd64 for Intel or AMD, arm64 for Apple silicon (Checkpoint 2).
  • Memory: 4 GB minimum, 8 GB recommended if your computer can spare it.
  • Processor cores: 2 or more.
  • Disk: 80 GB, dynamically allocated (it grows as it fills).
  • OS type, if your hypervisor asks: Linux, Debian 64-bit (ARM64 on Apple silicon).
  • Networking: NAT. Parallels and UTM call it Shared Network.
  • VM name and hostname: your abc123.
  • Kali account: username kali, password kali (Checkpoint 4).

content.title: No Preference? Use the Defaults
content.body: If you don’t care which tools you use, don’t spend time deciding: use Microsoft Copilot (free with your UTSA account) and VirtualBox (free). Still run the Find the right setup prompt and take Screenshot 01. If the answer says VirtualBox won’t run on your computer, go with what it recommends instead.

content.title: Pick Your AI Assistant
rows: UTSA turns it on for every student 18 or older. Sign in at copilot.microsoft.com with your @my.utsa.edu address and passphrase. Signed in, it has Microsoft’s enterprise data protection, so what you type isn’t used to train the AI. Details: utsa.edu/techsolutions/FacAndStaff/AI-Literacy/copilot-chat.html
Sign in with a Google account at gemini.google.com.
content.note: Each name links to the assistant’s own site. The free tier of any of these is plenty for this course. The accuracy stars come from our own testing: we ran this course’s AI Assist prompts through each assistant and had the answers graded for wrong facts and made-up sources. They reflect the specific model versions we tested in late 2026, so the app you open may score differently — treat the stars as a snapshot, not a promise. Copilot and ChatGPT were represented by the GPT model we could test. No assistant earned 5 stars: every one got some facts or sources wrong somewhere, which is exactly why you open and verify every source it hands you. The stars report what we found; they don’t tell you which assistant to pick. If you don’t have a favorite, start with Copilot.

The download needs a free Broadcom account, and Broadcom offers no support for the free version.

content.note: Each name links to its official download page (Hyper-V is built into Windows, so its link shows how to turn it on). Prices and support change. Check the official page before you pay for anything.

steps.text: Pick your AI assistant from the table above (no preference: Copilot). It’s the one you’ll paste the AI Assist prompts into, on this lab and the rest.

Find your computer’s specs: operating system and version, processor, memory and free disk space. Windows: Settings > System > About, and Settings > System > Storage for free space. Mac: Apple menu > About This Mac, and System Settings > General > Storage for free space.
Copy the Find the right setup prompt from the AI Assist card below into the AI assistant you use, fill in your specs and your budget, and send it.

Check it against the source of truth. Open the sources the AI listed and the hypervisor’s official page, and confirm three things yourself: it runs on your processor and operating system, what it costs, and that it can meet every requirement in What Your VM Has to Be. Where the AI and the official page disagree, the official page wins.
Take Screenshot 01 (below) before you move on.
Install the hypervisor you chose, using its official instructions. Kali keeps a guide for running Kali in each one: kali.org/docs/virtualization.
Open it to confirm it runs.

content.title: Trust the Source, Not the AI
content.body: An AI answer is a summary of what it has read, and it can be out of date or simply wrong while sounding completely sure. Prices change, supported chips change, menus get renamed. The source of truth is the original: the vendor’s official page, the tool’s documentation or man page, the standard itself, and in this course, the lab sheet. So use AI to get pointed in the right direction and to understand what you’re reading, then read the source and go by what it says. This is a habit analysts live by: nothing goes in a report because an AI said so, only because you checked it. In your EP 1 Runbook VM setup entry, next to Screenshot 01, name the official page you checked and anything the AI got wrong. That’s also the kind of example the AI Methodology Reflection asks for.

content.title: Screenshot
content.body: Capture your AI conversation showing the prompt with your computer’s specs and the AI’s recommendation. Your VM doesn’t exist yet, so this one is the exception to the abc123 rule. Save as 01-hypervisor-recommendation.png. It goes in your EP 1 Runbook, in the entry for your VM setup.

content.title: Common Pitfalls
items: Taking the AI’s word for it: if the recommendation says a hypervisor is free or supports your chip, confirm it on the official page before you install anything.
Describing your computer vaguely: an AI can only fit the recommendation to the computer you describe. “A laptop” gets you a generic answer.
Windows on ARM (Snapdragon) is the hard case: support for running Kali there is limited. Give the AI your exact processor and Windows edition, and expect it to point you to the arm64 image.
Virtualization turned off: if no hypervisor will start a VM, virtualization (Intel VT-x or AMD-V) has to be turned on in your BIOS/UEFI. Lab 1.0 shows how to check.
macOS blocking the install: allow the hypervisor in System Settings > Privacy & Security.

content.title: Getting Unstuck
content.body: Your hypervisor, your computer, your setup. There are too many combinations of hardware, operating systems and hypervisors for anyone to support them all, so setup problems are yours to solve, and AI is your first tool for solving them. That isn’t me being difficult. You have me for one semester, and after that you’ll be handed unfamiliar systems with nobody to ask, so start the habit now: when you’re stuck, ask an AI. Use the Decode my error prompt below: paste the exact error, say what you were doing, and tell it your setup. If the first answer doesn’t fix it, tell the AI what happened when you tried it and keep going. Still stuck after a real effort? Post the error and what you’ve tried in #module-1-help on Discord. Someone with the same setup may have already solved it.

content.title: Textbook Reference
content.body: Chapter 2 introduces defense in depth and the layered security model. Virtual machines provide isolation, a core security control that prevents testing activities from affecting production systems. Reading this chapter? That's a reference for your EP 1 report.

content.title: Dig Deeper
content.body: What’s the difference between Type 1 and Type 2 hypervisors? Find out where the one you chose falls in this classification, and why it matters for security testing.

content.whatYoureDoing: Downloading the Kali Linux installer image (~4GB) from the official source.
content.whyItMatters: Kali Linux is a Debian-based distribution designed specifically for penetration testing and security auditing. It comes pre-loaded with hundreds of security tools that you'll use throughout the semester for both offensive and defensive work.

steps.text: Navigate to kali.org/get-kali
Select Installer Images
Choose the correct architecture: 64-bit (amd64) for Intel/AMD processors, arm64 for Apple Silicon Macs (M1/M2/M3/M4). This depends on your processor, not your hypervisor.
Download the ISO file (approximately 4GB)
Note the download location; you'll need this for the next checkpoint

content.title: Time-Saving Tip
content.body: Start this download before working on other tasks. A 4GB download can take 10-30 minutes depending on your connection. You can proceed to review the remaining checkpoints while it downloads.

content.title: Common Pitfalls
items: Wrong architecture: Download the amd64 (64-bit) version unless you have Apple Silicon
Unofficial sources: Only download from kali.org; third-party ISOs may contain malware
Interrupted download: If download fails, delete partial file and restart; don't resume corrupted downloads

content.whatYoureDoing: Creating your virtual machine in the hypervisor you chose, to the requirements in Checkpoint 1.
content.whyItMatters: Proper VM configuration affects performance, stability, and functionality. The VM name is especially important. It appears in your terminal prompt and must be visible in screenshots for assignment verification.

steps.text: Copy the Tailor it to my setup prompt from the AI Assist card below into your AI assistant, fill in your computer and the hypervisor you chose, and send it. Keep its steps open while you work.
Create a new VM. Name your VM with your abc123, the ID you use to log into Canvas (for example, aaa000), not your Banner ID number. Just the ID: no prefix, no spaces.
If your hypervisor asks for the OS type: Linux, Debian 64-bit (ARM64 on Apple silicon).
Memory: 4 GB minimum, 8 GB recommended.
Processor cores: 2 or more.
Virtual disk: 80 GB, dynamically allocated.
Networking: NAT (Shared Network in Parallels and UTM).
Attach the Kali ISO from Checkpoint 2 as the VM’s startup disk (its CD/DVD drive).
Before you start the VM, check every setting against the requirements in Checkpoint 1. Where the AI’s steps differ from them, the requirements win.

content.title: Critical: VM Naming Convention
content.body: Name your VM <your abc123>, the ID you use to log into Canvas (for example, aaa000), not your Banner ID number. During the install you give Kali the same name as its hostname, so your abc123 shows in your terminal prompt (kali㉿aaa000) and in the VM window’s title bar. That is what verifies the screenshots are your own work; a VM named anything other than your ID makes your screenshots unverifiable.

content.title: Screenshot
content.body: Capture your VM’s settings window showing the VM name (your abc123), memory and processor count. Save as 02-vm-settings.png

content.title: Common Pitfalls
items: Leaving the placeholder name. Name your VM with your own abc123 (for example, aaa000), not the word abc123 and not your Banner ID number. This name must be visible in every screenshot.
Too little memory: 4 GB is the minimum, 8 GB is recommended; less makes Kali slow and unstable
ISO not attached: the VM won’t boot if the Kali ISO isn’t attached as its startup disk
Taking the AI’s word over the sheet: if its steps give a different name, less memory or another image, change it to match the requirements

content.title: Textbook Reference
content.body: Chapter 2 covers system resources and security considerations. Proper resource allocation ensures your testing environment performs reliably without impacting your host system's stability.

content.title: Dig Deeper
content.body: What are the VDI, VMDK, VHDX and qcow2 disk formats? Which one does your hypervisor use, and why do formats differ between hypervisors?

content.whatYoureDoing: Running the Kali Linux installer inside your virtual machine to create a functional security testing environment.
content.whyItMatters: Kali Linux comes pre-loaded with hundreds of security tools. A proper installation ensures all tools work correctly and the system is stable for the entire semester.

steps.text: Start the VM in your hypervisor
Select Graphical Install from the boot menu
Choose your language, location, and keyboard layout
Set the hostname to your abc123, exactly the same as your VM name (for example, aaa000). No prefix.
Leave domain name blank
Create the user account. Full name: kali. Username: kali. Password: kali (you type it twice).

whatThisDoes.concept: Yes, on purpose. We are building this for training, not production. Throw-away credentials are appropriate in a throw-away environment, and a VM you cannot log into is worth nothing to you. Every semester someone forgets the password they invented and has to rebuild the VM. Whether a security control applies depends on what the system is for, and recognizing that is the same judgment your Engagement Packets will ask you to make.

steps.text: Use Guided - use entire disk for partitioning
Select All files in one partition
Confirm and write changes to disk
Wait for installation to complete (15-25 minutes)
When the installer asks whether to install the GRUB boot loader, choose Yes. On the next screen, select your virtual hard disk (usually /dev/sda) as the boot loader device

whatThisDoes.concept: GRUB is the boot loader: the small program that starts Kali when the VM powers on. There are two questions, and both matter. Answer No, or skip choosing the disk, and the installer finishes but the VM cannot boot.

steps.text: Reboot when prompted

items: Inventing your own username or password: use kali for both. A forgotten password means rebuilding the VM
Wrong hostname: the hostname is your abc123, exactly the same as your VM name
Installation hangs: If stuck, check that VT-x/AMD-V is enabled in BIOS

content.title: What You Should Have
content.body: A fully installed Kali Linux system that boots to a graphical desktop. You should be able to log in as kali with the password kali.

content.title: Textbook Reference
content.body: Chapter 2 discusses operating system security and hardening. Understanding the installation process helps you make informed security decisions about system configuration.

content.whatYoureDoing: Installing Docker, the containerization platform we'll use to deploy vulnerable lab targets throughout the course.
content.whyItMatters: Docker lets us spin up isolated, vulnerable systems safely. Each module's client engagement uses Docker containers. Without it, you can't complete the labs.

steps.text: Update your package lists

whatThisDoes.concept: apt update refreshes the list of available packages from the repositories. It does not install anything. It just checks what's available. Always run this before installing new software so you get the latest versions.

steps.text: Upgrade all installed packages to current versions

whatThisDoes.concept: full-upgrade installs the newest versions of everything already on the system. Kali is a rolling release, so your ISO is a snapshot frozen at build time. This step brings your tools up to current. Use full-upgrade rather than plain upgrade: full-upgrade is allowed to add or remove packages to resolve dependency changes, so nothing gets held back. This is why your tool versions will match what the labs and quizzes expect.

steps.text: Install Docker and Docker Compose

whatThisDoes.concept: apt install downloads and installs packages. The -y flag automatically answers "yes" to the confirmation prompt. docker.io is the container engine; docker-compose lets you define multi-container environments in a single file.

steps.text: Enable Docker to start automatically and start it now

whatThisDoes.concept: systemctl enable tells the system to start Docker automatically on every boot. The --now flag also starts it immediately so you don't have to reboot first.

steps.text: Add your user to the Docker group

whatThisDoes.concept: usermod -aG appends your user to a group. By default, Docker commands require root access. Adding yourself to the docker group lets you run Docker without sudo every time.

steps.text: Log out of Kali and log back in (or reboot the VM) so the group change takes effect

whatThisDoes.concept: Your group memberships are read when you log in, so the terminal you already have open does not know you joined the docker group. Until you log out and back in, Docker commands without sudo fail with a permission error.

content.title: Pro Tip
content.body: After adding yourself to the docker group, you must log out and back in (or reboot) for the group membership to take effect. Until then, you'll need sudo for docker commands.

steps.text: Check the Docker version

whatThisDoes.output: You should see the installed Docker version number. If you get "command not found", the installation didn't complete correctly.

steps.text: Run the Docker test container

whatThisDoes.concept: docker run pulls an image from Docker Hub and runs it as a container. The hello-world image is a tiny test container that prints a success message. If you see "Hello from Docker!", Docker is fully working.
whatThisDoes.output: You should see "Hello from Docker!" followed by a short explanation of what Docker just did. If you get "permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket", you haven't logged out and back in since adding yourself to the docker group. Do that, then run this command again.

content.title: Screenshot
content.body: Capture docker --version and the hello-world output. Save as 04-docker-version.png

content.title: Common Pitfalls
items: Permission denied: You didn't log out after adding yourself to the docker group
Cannot connect to daemon: Docker service isn't running; check with sudo systemctl status docker
Network errors: VM needs internet access; check your hypervisor’s network settings (it should be NAT)

content.title: Dig Deeper
content.body: What's the difference between a container and a virtual machine? Research how Docker’s architecture differs from a hypervisor and why containers are preferred for deploying applications.

content.title: Textbook Reference
content.body: Chapter 2 covers defense in depth and isolation as a security control. Docker uses Linux kernel features (namespaces and cgroups) to create lightweight isolation without a full hypervisor. Containers and VMs represent two different points on the isolation spectrum that security professionals choose between based on their threat model.

content.whatYoureDoing: Running a series of commands to verify your environment is properly configured and all required tools are available.
content.whyItMatters: Catching configuration issues now prevents frustration later. A working baseline environment means you can focus on learning security concepts instead of troubleshooting setup problems.

steps.text: Display your hostname

whatThisDoes.output: This should show your abc123 (for example, aaa000). If it shows kali, the word abc123, or any name that isn’t your ID, fix it before proceeding.

steps.text: Display kernel and OS information

whatThisDoes.concept: uname -a prints all system information: kernel name, hostname, kernel version, architecture. The -a flag means "all." This is a standard first step when documenting an engagement environment.

content.title: Screenshot
content.body: Capture the Part A output: hostname and uname -a, with your hostname visible in the prompt. Save as 05-system-verification.png

steps.text: Display your network interfaces and IP addresses

whatThisDoes.concept: ip addr lists all network interfaces and their assigned IP addresses. Look for your eth0 interface. It should have an IP address from your hypervisor’s NAT network (the range depends on the hypervisor; VirtualBox uses 10.0.2.x).

steps.text: Test internet connectivity

whatThisDoes.concept: ping sends ICMP echo requests to test network reachability. The -c 3 flag limits it to 3 packets. 8.8.8.8 is Google's public DNS. If all 3 packets come back, you have internet connectivity.

content.title: Screenshot
content.body: Capture the Part B output: ip addr and the ping results showing all 3 packets received. Your hostname must be visible. Save as 06-network-connectivity.png

steps.text: Verify Nmap is installed

whatThisDoes.concept: Nmap is the industry-standard network scanner. You'll use it heavily starting in Module 1 Lab 2. The --version flag confirms it's installed and shows the version number.

steps.text: Verify Wireshark is installed

whatThisDoes.concept: Wireshark is a packet capture and analysis tool. You'll use it in Module 3 to inspect network traffic.

steps.text: Verify John the Ripper is installed

whatThisDoes.concept: John the Ripper is a password cracking tool you'll use in Module 4. The | head -5 pipe takes the first 5 lines of output, enough to confirm it's installed without flooding your terminal.

steps.text: Confirm Docker version
Verify no containers are running yet

whatThisDoes.concept: docker ps lists running containers. Right now it should show an empty table (just headers). In later modules, this is how you'll confirm your lab target containers are running before you start scanning.

content.body: Capture the Part C and Part D output: the Nmap, Wireshark and John the Ripper version checks, docker --version, and the empty docker ps table. Your hostname must be visible. Save as 07-tool-verification.png

content.title: Textbook Reference

items.label: Isolated Attack Platforms
items.text: Virtual machines let attackers operate from a clean, disposable environment. After an engagement, the VM can be rolled back or deleted, leaving no artifacts on the analyst’s host.

items.label: Container Recon Targets
items.text: Docker containers are everywhere in modern infrastructure. Understanding how they run and expose ports is essential for finding attack surface in containerized environments.

items.label: Tool Availability
items.text: Kali Linux pre-loads every tool you’ll use this semester. Attackers maintain their own customized distributions. Having a ready toolkit is a force multiplier.

items.label: Environment Hygiene
items.text: Defenders use virtualization the same way: isolated sandboxes for malware analysis, forensics, and safe tool testing. Understanding the tech from both sides makes you a better analyst.

items.label: Container Security Posture
items.text: Every port mapped in docker run is a potential attack surface. Defenders must understand container networking to audit what’s actually exposed.

items.label: Documentation Discipline
items.text: Blue teamers live and die by documentation. Building the habit of capturing and naming screenshots in Unit 1 reflects how real SOC analysts maintain evidence chains.

purpleTeam.connection: Your lab environment is both your attack platform and your first blue team lesson. Every security professional (red or blue) maintains an isolated, documented, reproducible workspace. This setup is that workspace.
